chunks: But he who says to his parents: "Shame on you: You intimidate me that I will be resurrected when many generations will have passed before me?" And (the parents) would implore God's help: "Woe to you. You better believe. The promise of God is certainly true." Yet he answers: "These are only fables of long ago."

key_terms.أُفٍّ: An expression of slight impatience or contempt
key_terms.وَيْلَكَ: Woe to you (an expression of warning)
key_terms.يَسْتَغِيثَانِ: They implore for help or seek aid

ai.seo_question: Who is the person that said 'Uff' to his parents regarding resurrection in Surah Ad-Dhariyat?
ai.summary: In Surah Al-Ahqaf, this verse highlights the archetype of the disbelieving son who counters his pious parents' exhortations with empirical skepticism, arguing that since previous generations have perished, resurrection is impossible. Shia exegetes often view this as a critique of rationalist denial of the afterlife, where the parents' plea for 'Aman' (belief) underscores the necessity of accepting divine promise despite logical doubts, while the son's dismissal as 'Asatir al-Awwalin' (fables of old) reflects a common Qur'anic motif for denying prophetic truths.
